facts.label: scripture
facts.quote: These refer to the creation of Kerala by the legendary hero Parasurama, who is supposed to have hurled his battle-axe from Gokarna to Cape Comorin and claimed from the sea all the land in between.
facts.text: According to the Kerala Mahatmya, the sage Parashurama hurled his battle-axe into the ocean from Gokarna to Kanyakumari to reclaim the coastal tract of Kerala from the sea deity Varuna.

facts.label: scripture
facts.quote: According to the Sahyadri Khanda of the Skanda Purana, Lord Parshuram shot his arrow into the sea and commanded the sea god Varuna to recede up to the point where his arrow landed.
facts.text: The Sahyadri Khanda of the Skanda Purana relates that Parashurama shot an arrow from the Sahyadri crest into the sea, compelling the waters to withdraw and form the coastal region of Konkan.

facts.label: scripture
facts.quote: To people this land, Parasurama is said to have first brought a poor Brahman... Other Brahmans are next brought and located in sixty-four gramas or villages.
facts.text: The Malayalam traditional chronicle Keralolpatti asserts that Parashurama settled the newly reclaimed coastal territory by allocating land across 64 Brahmin gramams.

facts.label: scripture
facts.quote: In the sacrifice he gave all the lands as alms to Brahmins, which was received by Kasyapa... Accordingly Parasurama created new land by shooting an arrow at the sea, for his own use.
facts.text: The Mahabharata states in the Drona Parva that after gifting all conquered lands to sage Kashyapa, Parashurama caused the ocean to recede to obtain a personal sanctuary.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: This linear strip of land is bounded by the Western Ghats on the east and the Arabian sea on the west... Of the 560 km shoreline of Kerala, a cumulative 360 km length of shoreline is vulnerable and shows wide fluctuations in its stability.
facts.source_name: Geological Survey of India, Miscellaneous Publication No. 30
facts.text: Modern geological mapping defines Kerala's coastal plain along a shoreline extending roughly 590 km between the Western Ghats and the Arabian Sea.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: Quaternary sediments of Kerala form relatively thin unconsolidated horizons lying unconformably over the older rocks with an areal distribution of about 3000 sq km.
facts.source_name: Geological Survey of India, Miscellaneous Publication No. 30
facts.text: Geological Survey of India investigations mapped the Quaternary Kadappuram Formation, composed of marine and beach sand complexes covering an area of approximately 3000 sq km along the Kerala coast.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: The 14C ages reported for the present-day onshore peat and shell material at various depths along the SW coast of India reveal that after 6400 yr BP, the sea level receded and stabilized at the present level.
facts.text: Radiocarbon dating of onshore peat and shell horizons along southwestern India demonstrated that regional sea levels receded and reached modern stability following a high stand around 6400 years Before Present.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: Three of the eight vibrocores within the innershelf at depths of 18 to 23 m have struck a peat horizon.
facts.source_name: Geological Survey of India Marine Wing
facts.text: Geological Survey of India marine cores drilled at depths between 18 and 23 metres off southern Kerala struck a submerged peat bed formed during early Holocene subaerial conditions.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: Vambanad Lake – 205 km2, developed due to transgression-regression activities linked with sea level change and surrounded by recent sediments.
facts.text: Geomorphological surveys show that the 205 square kilometre Vembanad lagoon basin developed due to marine transgression-regression cycles that formed barrier spits during the late Quaternary.

facts.label: disputed
facts.quote: It is observed that the evolution of coastal landforms is influenced by the fall in sea level and/or uplift of the coast... the fault lineaments parallel to the coast as well as those at right angles to it are found to be neotectonically active.
facts.source_name: Journal of Geological Society of India (M. M. Nair)
facts.text: Geologists debate whether the emergence of Kerala's coastal strip was primarily driven by neotectonic vertical uplift of the coastline or by global eustatic sea-level fall and riverine sediment accretion.

facts.label: disputed
facts.quote: William Logan, the author of the Malabar Manual (1887), also refutes the validity of the Keralolpathi and describes it as follows: 'a farrago of legendary nonsense having for its definite aim the securing of the Brahmin caste of unbounded power and influence in the country'.
facts.text: Historians such as William Logan argued that the Parashurama reclamation tale was a medieval myth engineered to legitimize land grants, whereas some modern analysts argue it reflects an authentic folk memory of mid-Holocene sea recession.

facts.label: legend
facts.quote: Parashurama invoked forth the mighty Naagaraja Vasuki, who spat forth holy poison that transformed the salty sterile land into a lush, verdant paradise.
facts.text: Oral folklore across Kerala and Tulu Nadu holds that the serpent king Vasuki sprayed divine poison onto the newly emerged salty seabed to neutralize its salt and turn the soil fertile.

The background is real and in motion behind him (as fits the place: waves, mist, leaves, flags, lamps flickering, people walking, traffic, light shifting); never a still, flat or heavily blurred backdrop. If the scene shows the past, it is ancient India: Indian people in dhotis, sarees and angavastram, warriors with bows, spears and bronze or leather armour, carved stone pillars, oil lamps; never European knights, plate armour, castles or anything medieval European. Movement and framing: like a TV news reporter on location, he walks toward the camera while he speaks: he starts three or four steps back, seen from the knees up, walks steadily and confidently toward the lens, and stops at a medium shot from the waist up for the last words. His whole head and both shoulders stay inside the frame the whole time, with clear space above his hair and on both sides; do not crop the top of his head. Lighting: warm key light on the face, a soft rim light on the hair, matched to the scene; flattering, no harsh shadows, no dull or flat grey look. SG [locked] walking tall and lively, shoulders open, energetic and confident, wearing a mustard kurta. Speaks from the first frame, mouth matched to the words, steady eye contact with the lens. Face and delivery: an excited, high-energy presenter breaking a big story, full of life, as if he cannot wait to tell you. Bright, wide-awake eyes, lively eyebrows that lift on the question, a big, bright, genuine smile. On the question his voice rises with excitement as he strides closer. On the last line a big confident smile, a quick nod and a point at the viewer. Natural blinking, lively head movement. Never sad, gloomy, worried, tired, sleepy, flat or bored; never a frown, never a blank face. Voice: energetic, upbeat, punchy and clear, a brisk pace, rising on the question, with a quick beat before the last line. Hands: energetic, natural gestures at chest height: a quick point toward the scene behind him on the question and an open palm toward the viewer on the last line; never limp, never hanging still by his sides. Camera: eye level, steady, holding its place as he walks up to it (a very slight slow push-in at most), slight handheld feel.
